title: Francis of Paola (2 April)
hook: a hermit whose motto was charity, who named his brothers the least

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dismas, the thief on the cross who asked only to be remembered. Your line was remember me. Who did you remember behind bars? Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

A dying king sends for a hermit. The king is Louis the Eleventh of France, powerful, frightened, and sick. He has heard that a holy man in the south of Italy works wonders, and he wants one. He sends messengers, gifts, promises. The hermit, a man named Francis from the little town of Paola, does not want to go. He goes only when the pope tells him to. He makes the long journey to France, walks into the royal court in his rough habit, and stands at the bedside of a king who wants a miracle. Today, what the hermit gave him instead.
screen: `A DYING KING SENDS FOR A HERMIT.` → `HE GOES ONLY WHEN THE POPE ASKS.` → `A KING WANTS A MIRACLE.`

segments.voice: Francis didn't cure the king. Tradition says he stayed with him, prayed with him, and helped him get ready to die in peace. Then he stayed on in France for the rest of his own life, and, tradition says, the French court kept asking his advice. To see why that matters, go back to the start. As a young man Francis went off alone to live as a hermit in a cave near the sea. Other young men came to join him, and slowly a community grew. He gave them a name meant to keep them low: the Minims. Tradition says he chose it to mean the least of all, lower even than Francis of Assisi's Friars Minor, the lesser brothers. And he gave them one word as a motto, written on their badge: Charity. Love. The Minims kept a life of Lent all year round, with no meat and plain food, not to be grim, but to stay light and free for others. Behind the name sits a line from the Gospel of Matthew, where Jesus speaks of the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner. In the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." The least ones are where Christ says he will be found. Francis wanted his brothers to stand among them, not above them. Even in a palace. Especially in a palace. The hermit at the king's bed was there as the least man in the room.
screen: `HE DIDN'T CURE THE KING.` · `A HERMIT IN A CAVE BY THE SEA.` · `THE MINIMS: THE LEAST OF ALL.` · `ONE WORD ON THE BADGE: CHARITY.` · then, large: `ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one least thing. Settle, and breathe. Francis's brothers took the lowest place on purpose. Ask yourself what the smallest, least noticed job around you is today. The dishes nobody wants. The trash bin at the curb. The coworker everyone talks past. The text you've been putting off to someone lonely. Pick one. Not a grand gesture. A least one, done without needing anyone to notice. If you pray, you can offer it with the word on the Minims' badge: charity. If you don't, simply hold the task in mind. The bell holds the time.
Minims, the least brothers, founded by Francis of Paola. A hermit who gave them charity as their motto, and sat at a dying king's bed.
Your line: the least ones. Today, do your one least thing, and let nobody thank you for it. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Francis of Paola's optional memorial on 2 April; the Minim friars, nuns and lay members who follow his rule still keep a Lenten diet all year.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, ages or counts spoken (his age entering the hermitage, Louis XI's death year, the year of his own death, the number of houses).
'Minims' as 'the least of all' and its relation to the Friars Minor given as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Motto 'Charitas' on the order's emblem: tradition (some accounts say shown to him by St. Michael). Confirm phrasing 'written on their badge'.

Louis XI: summoned him hoping for a cure; Francis went at the order of Pope Sixtus IV; he did not cure him and attended his death. Confirm 'he goes only when the pope tells him to' and 'kings kept coming to him for advice' (Charles VIII, Louis XII).
Fourth vow of Lenten life (abstaining from meat, eggs, dairy): simplified to 'no meat and plain food'. Confirm howItsDone wording about present-day Minims.
